    Build MultiSolid from a checkout

    Build on the operating system you want to run: Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64 with Python 3.12, or Windows 11 x64 with Python 3.11. These are the pinned desktop build environments; this is not a cross-compilation recipe. Source development still supports Python 3.11 and 3.12.

    Clone the repository, install the prerequisites below, then run one command from the repository root. You do not need to activate a virtual environment. The builder creates its own environment, installs hash-pinned Python packages, downloads verified DAETools and native inputs, builds the compiler/solver bundle, stages Graphviz, builds application wheels, freezes the desktop, tests a relocated copy, and packages it. Allow several GB of disk space and time for downloads and the first native build. No administrator privileges are needed after installing the system prerequisites.

    Linux

    On Ubuntu 24.04, install the build and GUI dependencies:

    sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y python3.12 python3.12-venv build-essential gfortran cmake binutils \
  graphviz fonts-dejavu-core libxcb-cursor0 libxkbcommon-x11-0 libxcb-icccm4 \
  libxcb-image0 libxcb-keysyms1 libxcb-render-util0 libxcb-xinerama0 libxcb-randr0 \
  libxcb-shape0 libxcb-xfixes0 libxcb-sync1 libxcb-xkb1 libgl1 libegl1 \
  libfontconfig1 libdbus-1-3 xvfb xauth
python3.12 tools/build_desktop.py --headless

    --headless uses Xvfb with Qt's real X11 backend. From a graphical desktop you can omit it to see the acceptance-test windows. The build fails early if a required Qt library is missing; libxcb-cursor0 is required even for headless X11 validation. Other distributions need equivalent packages and their own qualification. The automatic Graphviz collector currently supports Debian/Ubuntu.

    The finished download is under dist/linux/releases/. Extract the entire MultiSolid-<version>-linux-x64-portable.tar.gz, then run MultiSolid/MultiSolid. The archive includes Python, DAETools, Qt, Graphviz, the compiler and solver libraries. See Linux details for compatibility and manual steps.

    Windows

    Install CPython 3.11.9 x64, Git, and MSYS2. In the MSYS2 UCRT64 terminal, install the native build tools (including the separately packaged OpenMP runtime):

    pacman -S --needed mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-libgomp mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-cmake mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-ninja

    Then use PowerShell, from the repository root:

    $env:PATH = "C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin;$env:PATH"
py -3.11 tools/build_desktop.py

    Adjust C:\msys64 if you installed MSYS2 elsewhere. Use ordinary Windows Python, not MSYS2 Python. Keep MSYS2's package licence files installed: staging includes them with the native runtime. DAETools, Zig, and the pinned Windows Graphviz archives are downloaded automatically.

    The finished download is dist/windows/releases/MultiSolid-<version>-windows-x64-portable.zip. Extract it completely, then run MultiSolid/MultiSolid.exe. To also create the per-user installer, install Inno Setup 6.7.3 and add its compiler:

    py -3.11 tools/build_desktop.py --iscc 'C:\Program Files (x86)\Inno Setup 6\ISCC.exe'

    The existing Windows release guide describes manual staging, installer qualification, and release records. Its PowerShell release wrapper continues to work for environments staged by hand.

    Caches, inputs and troubleshooting

    • Work files and logs are under build/release-linux/ or build/release-windows/. --work PATH and --output PATH choose another build cache and distribution directory. Use a new work directory when changing Python versions or toolchains.
    • --jobs 4 controls native build parallelism. Use fewer jobs on small machines.
    • --daetools PATH accepts an extracted DAETools 2.6.0 release or a matching wheel when you already have it. Native extensions must match the build Python version and include SuperLU and Trilinos. The official releases are linked at DAETools downloads (online).
    • --compiled-bundle PATH and --graphviz-bundle PATH reuse prepared bundles. The freezer still checks Linux runtime relocation and GUI dependencies.
    • Downloads are cached and hash checked. For a checksum mismatch, remove the named archive and retry; do not bypass verification. A failed or interrupted build can be rerun. Application wheels are rebuilt each time.
    • Keep the build environment separate from your development environment. Extra Python packages can affect PyInstaller discovery. The supplied command owns its dedicated venv; use the low-level tools for custom environments.
    • acceptance-*/check/validation.json records validation for the exact bundle. A failure leaves logs beside that file and prevents packaging. The acceptance test covers simulations, concurrent workers, caches, reports, project archives, cancellation, external plugins, and paths with spaces/Unicode.
    • Release checks remove developer compiler, Python, Graphviz and library paths. Linux runs must not need an LD_LIBRARY_PATH workaround. A missing SUNDIALS library usually means an old native bundle needs rebuilding/restaging.

    SHA256SUMS.txt, release.json, BUILD-INFO.json, and bundle-files.json identify the artifacts. Retain the sources, downloaded inputs and validation logs when distributing a build. Always qualify the final extracted archive on a clean target machine; a passing build-host check does not establish support for every Linux distribution or Windows configuration.
